title: Evaluating Prompt-Injection and Retrieval/Tool-Channel Attacks on Agentic NetOps Pipelines and Layered Defenses
abstract: Problem: Agentic LLM pipelines for NetOps expose retrieval and tool channels that adversaries can exploit via prompt injection. Method: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing an unguarded agentic NetOps pipeline (baseline) against a defense-in-depth configuration (RAG grounding with provenance + deterministic runtime validator + sandboxed tool outputs). Design: 80 task seeds × 2 model families planned (paired design); confirmatory contrast = baseline vs combined defense; deterministic parsing and provenance checks; preregistration and all artifacts frozen and hashed. Key result (confirmatory): among 150 complete paired runs, baseline attack-success = 147/150 (98.0%), guarded attack-success = 150/150 (100.0%); guarded − baseline = +0.02 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.0467]); McNemar two-sided p = 0.25 (paired analysis). Major limitation: results are limited to the two hosted-model families, the simulated NetOps semantics and the implemented validator/RAG/sandbox; missing/infrastructure failures reduced the analyzed pairs to 150 (10 preregistered pairs unavailable). Conclusion: in this controlled NetOps simulation, the implemented defense-in-depth did not produce a statistically detectable reduction in attack-success; further work needed on defense design, broader model coverage, and real-device evaluation. All data, code, prompts, and hashes are published in the execution artifacts referenced below.

sections.introduction: Agentic LLM systems promise intent-driven automation for network operations (NetOps) but expand the attack surface for prompt-injection through retrieval and tool channels. Prior work has documented indirect prompt injection and agentic attack surfaces and proposed defense-in-depth architectures (preregistered evidence set referenced below). We studied whether a layered defensive configuration (trusted-source filtering + RAG with provenance + deterministic runtime validator + sandboxed tool outputs) reduces adversarial-injection success in an agentic NetOps pipeline under a preregistered paired design. The research question: How effective are retrieval- and tool-channel prompt-injection attacks against an agentic NetOps pipeline, and to what extent does the defense-in-depth configuration reduce attack success?
sections.related_work: We positioned the study against verified literature on prompt injection and agentic LLM agents, RAG/grounding approaches, generate-verify-repair patterns, and runtime/shielding defenses. Representative verified sources used to motivate design and defenses are listed in the cited_record_ids field and the preregistration evidence record. The study is experimental and narrowly scoped to attack–defense interactions in a simulator-executable NetOps semantics layer.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: study cnsmautocand-2-v1 with frozen design (paired confirmatory contrast, inclusion/exclusion rules, parser and provenance checks, seeds, retry policy). Pipeline: public hosted LLM APIs (two model families: OpenAI GPT-4 family and Anthropic Claude-2 family per preregistration), deterministic prompt templates and parser modules (artifact paths recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and hashed in execution/artifact_hashes). Conditions: baseline (unguarded agentic pipeline), RAG-only, validator-only, combined (RAG+validator+sandbox). Primary estimand: relative reduction in attack-success proportion for combined defense vs baseline (paired per task-model unit). Planned runs: 80 seeds × 2 model families = 160 paired units (preregistration). Execution: automated runs recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl, scoring artifacts in execution/scoring/*.json, provenance and provider-call logs published; retries only for infrastructure/API failures (one automatic retry), infrastructure failures logged. Deterministic parsing mapped LLM outputs to canonical CLI ASTs; parser failures and provenance mismatches excluded from confirmatory analysis per preregistered rules.
sections.results: Execution manifest: planned_episode_count=320, completed_episode_count=300, failed_episode_count=20, model_calls_used=163 (detailed hashes in execution/artifact_hashes). Missingness: 10 preregistered paired units were unavailable for the confirmatory analysis and excluded per preregistered rules. Confirmatory analysis (complete pairs n=150): baseline attack-success 147/150 (98.0%), guarded (combined defense) attack-success 150/150 (100.0%). Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = +0.02; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.0466667]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.25. Interpretation: the implemented combined defense did not produce a statistically significant reduction in attack-success in this experiment; the point estimate indicates no reduction and a numerically small increase in realized attack-success under the guarded configuration in the analyzed pairs. No secondary confirmatory contrasts met preregistered confirmatory status; exploratory stratified summaries and audit tables are provided in the artifact bundle.
sections.discussion: The confirmatory outcome indicates that, for the implemented RAG+validator+sandbox pipeline and the adversarial corpus used, the combined defense did not measurably lower attack-success. Possible operational interpretations (consistent with preregistered scope) include: (1) adversarial payloads exploited channels or phrasing that bypassed the validator predicates or RAG grounding in this prototype; (2) model behavior under deterministic sampling (temperature=0.0 per preregistration) still produced dangerous outputs that the deterministic validator did not classify as violations; (3) simulation semantics and parser acceptance criteria permit attackful actions that a production validator might block. These interpretations are exploratory and require further empirical testing. All raw runs, provenance traces, parser outputs, and analysis scripts are published in the artifact bundle for independent reanalysis.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered, paired confirmatory study of prompt-injection against an agentic NetOps prototype, the specific defense-in-depth configuration implemented (RAG with provenance + deterministic runtime validator + sandboxed tool outputs) did not reduce attack-success relative to an unguarded baseline in the analyzed runs (n=150 pairs). The result cautions that defense composition and validator design matter; additional research should widen model coverage, strengthen deterministic validators and provenance policies, and evaluate on richer NetOps semantics and real-device contexts. All experimental artifacts and analyses are published to enable replication and follow-up.

limitations: Limited model coverage: only two hosted-model families (preregistered) were exercised; results do not generalize to other LLM families or model versions.

Simulator semantics: the NetOps semantics and validators ran in a simulator-executable environment (no live-device deployment); simulator-model mismatch could alter operational effectiveness in production.
Implementation-specific defenses: the RAG, validator predicates, and sandbox were prototype implementations; different defense designs or stronger predicates might yield different outcomes.

Sample and missingness: confirmatory analysis used 150 complete paired runs (10 preregistered pairs unavailable); failed/infrastructure episodes (20) and excluded pairs reduce effective sample and statistical precision.

Parser and mapping dependence: the analysis required deterministic parsing of LLM outputs to CLI ASTs; parser failures and mapping thresholds affect inclusion and are a potential construct-validity threat.

Attack-corpus and task scope: the adversarial corpus and four NetOps task clusters (ACL modification, route advertisement change, firewall-rule insertion, interface/route shutdown) are not exhaustive of NetOps actions or attack techniques.

External validity: results are limited to the studied pipeline, attack corpus, and simulation settings; production environments with different retrieval sources, tool integrations, or operator oversight may behave differently.
